articles.title: Xen Orchestra flaws exploited as unlogged access complicates investigation
articles.excerpt: Xen Orchestra vulnerabilities are being exploited, while unauthorized access is not logged, according to SecurityWeek’s reporting of a Vates warning. This limits what defenders can conclude from missi…
articles.body: Xen Orchestra vulnerabilities are being exploited, while unauthorized access is not logged, according to SecurityWeek’s reporting of a Vates warning. This limits what defenders can conclude from missing access records: their absence does not establish that a system is safe. Affected versions and potential impact Vates warned that a threat actor is exploiting a critical authentication bypass alongside a zero-day vulnerability. The authentication flaw exposes reusable login token IDs, allowing an unauthenticated attacker to gain administrative privileges. The authentication flaw affects Xen Orchestra versions before 6.9.2 on the stable branch and before 6.10.1 on the latest branch, as well as Xen Orchestra Appliance installations containing the affected software.

articles.title: Instrumenting Keyright license verification with OpenTelemetry: the metrics, traces, and tags that matter
articles.excerpt: You have an ActivitySource around your outbound HTTP calls, a histogram on your database round-trips, and a dashboard that lights up the moment your payment provider gets slow. Then look at the one ca…
articles.body: You have an ActivitySource around your outbound HTTP calls, a histogram on your database round-trips, and a dashboard that lights up the moment your payment provider gets slow. Then look at the one call that decides whether your software is allowed to run tonight — the license verification — and it is almost always a blind spot. It fails, it slows down, it quietly starts serving every customer from a cached lease because your Keyright instance is briefly unreachable, and the first anyone hears of it is a support ticket. A license check is a dependency call. It deserves the same treatment as any other: a metric you can alert on and a span you can read when one activation is mysteriously slow.

articles.title: Shipping Verifiable Agents for zkVerify #AgentGames: Proof Gatekeeper, Steal the VFY, and zkGuard
articles.excerpt: Most Web3 agents still run on "trust the server." An endpoint tells you it checked a payment request or screened a transaction for drainers, and you have no way to verify what logic actually ran. For…
articles.body: Most Web3 agents still run on "trust the server." An endpoint tells you it checked a payment request or screened a transaction for drainers, and you have no way to verify what logic actually ran. For zkVerify #AgentGames , I built and deployed two agent services: 0xginn ( zkverify-agent ) , a dual-track agent competing in Proof Gatekeeper and Steal the VFY . zkGuard ( zkguard-wildcard ) , a pre-signing EVM/BSC transaction guard for the Wildcard track. Instead of letting an LLM make the final call, both services separate request parsing from deterministic policy code and attach a Groth16 proof ( snarkjs on BN128) to every verdict. 1. Transport and Auth First Every request to /agent is signed by the platform with x-agent-games-signature .

articles.body: Disclosure up front: I build ToolKnit, and this post is about how its PDF to Word converter got local OCR for scanned pages. I'm writing it because the hard parts were more about honesty and UX than about algorithms. Constraint: the document never leaves the device The goal was a DOCX from a text PDF or a scanned one, with no upload, no account and no AI key. That rules out sending pages to a cloud OCR API. Everything has to run in the tab. 1. Native text first, OCR second If a PDF already has a text layer, OCR only adds errors. The engine reads text and drawing instructions first, using positions and font information to rebuild reading order, columns and tables. OCR only runs on pages that are really just images. 2.

Both forms were the same security (one ISIN, two trading codes) and cleared at one weighted average yield: 15.72%. The governor said on 13 November that tokenized government bonds will "probably" follow in Q1 2027. Spend Node's write-up of the auction results gives two more numbers: executed tokenized orders came to about 9.62 billion tenge against 10 billion nominal, and total proceeds were about 48.11 billion tenge. articles.title: On this day in space! Nov. 15, 1988: The 300-foot Green Bank Telescope collapses suddenly, leaving a huge pile of wreckage in West Virginia
articles.excerpt: On Nov. 15, 1988, a 300-foot radio telescope in Green Bank, West Virginia suddenly collapsed. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Nov. 15, 1988, a 300-foot radio telescope in Green Bank, West Virginia suddenly collapsed. It happened at 9:46 p.m. on a clear night with no strong winds. When the observatory staff showed up to work the next morning, they were greeted by a huge pile of wreckage. The telescope collapsed under its own weight after a key structural element called a "gusset plate" failed. This was one of four connecting plates that held the telescope's large, metal beams together. Investigators found that these gusset plates were not built to last the 26 years that this telescope had been in use. Three years later, construction began on a new telescope. The Green Bank Telescope was even bigger and more sensitive, and it began science operations in 2001.

articles.body: For the past two years, stargazers have waited with bated breath for a "new" light to appear in the night sky, born of one of the most cataclysmic events known to occur in the cosmos — a nova explosion. But what is the "Blaze Star" T. Coronae Borealis, and why is it so difficult to predict when its overdue brightening will occur? We turned to the experts to find out. What is T. Coronae Borealis? T. Coronae Borealis — or T CrB for short — isn't a single star, but rather a binary system containing a dense white dwarf star and a bloated red giant. Over a period of around 80 years, the white dwarf's gravity strips material from the red giant until it hits a critical threshold.

articles.title: How escaping gases ripped apart a comet and caused it to become thousands of times brighter
articles.excerpt: This summer, comet 220P/McNaught burst into life out of nowhere to become one of the year’s highlights for amateur astronomers.
articles.body: A comet dazzled this summer as the sun’s heat caused ice beneath its surface to turn to gas and rip out through its surface, spewing hundreds of billions of pounds' worth of dust into space and causing the comet to brighten by thousands of times. Comet 220P/McNaught was discovered by the prolific Australian comet discoverer Robert McNaught in 2004. It is a periodic comet, the 220th discovered, meaning that it comes back again and again on a regular basis – in 220P’s case, once every five-and-a-half years when it gets about as close to the sun as Mars . Other than that, 220P is fairly nondescript, usually languishing at a feeble brightness fainter than magnitude +15, out of reach of most amateur telescopes. There has been little else to say about the comet, until this year.

articles.title: What's next for SpaceX's Starship after epic Flight 15 chopsticks catch?
articles.excerpt: SpaceX just made spaceflight history, catching the upper stage of its Starship megarocket when it returned to Earth. But Starship still has some pretty big boxes left to check.
articles.body: Starship may have just made history, but it still has some work to do to get fully up and running. The megarocket launched on its 15th test flight on Friday (Nov. 13), aiming to pull off a dramatic and unprecedented twofer. SpaceX wanted to bring both Starship elements — its Super Heavy booster and Ship upper stage — back to the launch pad at its Starbase site in Texas to be caught by the tower's "chopstick" arms. It didn't happen with Super Heavy; the booster diverted to a Gulf of Mexico splashdown on Friday evening after experiencing a low-fuel alarm. But Ship came home successfully , nestling into the tower's arms in a soft and unprecedented embrace on Saturday afternoon (Nov. 14), 22.5 hours after lifting off. Long-distance view of Ship's historic landing on Nov. 14, 2026.
